questions.explanation: An async method runs *synchronously* until its first `await` on something incomplete, so "B" prints straight away. At `await Task.Delay` it returns an incomplete Task to the caller, which prints "C", then awaits the task: "D" after the delay, then "E".

questions.prompt: What should an async method return if it produces no value (and isn't an event handler)?
questions.explanation: Return `Task` so callers can await it and observe exceptions. `async void` can't be awaited and its exceptions crash the process, so reserve it for event handlers. `Task<void>` doesn't exist.

questions.prompt: Blocking on a Task with `.Result` or `.Wait()` on a UI thread (which has a synchronization context) commonly causes what problem?
questions.explanation: The UI thread blocks waiting for the task, but the task's continuation is queued to resume *on the UI thread*, which is blocked. Neither can proceed. The fix is to use `await` all the way up rather than blocking.

questions.prompt: Which code starts three independent downloads concurrently and waits for all of them to finish?
questions.explanation: `Task.WhenAll` takes the already-started tasks and completes when all are done, returning all results. Awaiting one at a time runs them sequentially. `WhenAny` completes when the *first* finishes. `.Result` inside `Select` blocks on each in turn: sequential, and deadlock-prone.

questions.prompt: Which call on an awaited Task tells it not to resume on the captured synchronization context (common advice for library code)?
questions.explanation: `await task.ConfigureAwait(false)` lets the continuation run on any thread-pool thread instead of marshalling back to the original context (e.g. the UI thread). It avoids needless context switches and the classic sync-over-async deadlock in library code. ASP.NET Core has no synchronization context, so it matters less there.

questions.prompt: Does `await` by itself start a new thread?
distractors: Yes, always on a thread-pool thread
questions.explanation: `await` just pauses the method until the task completes and schedules the rest as a continuation. For I/O there's often *no* thread waiting at all. A new thread-pool work item only appears if something like `Task.Run` created one.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism?
questions.answer: Concurrency is several tasks in progress over overlapping time (they may interleave on one thread, like async I/O); parallelism is several literally running at the same instant on multiple cores.
distractors: Parallelism is for I/O-bound work; concurrency is for CPU-bound work.
Concurrency needs multiple threads; parallelism can happen on one thread.
questions.explanation: Parallelism is one way to be concurrent. Async/await gives concurrency for I/O-bound work (many requests in flight, few threads); `Parallel.For` and PLINQ give parallelism for CPU-bound work.

questions.prompt: Which method queues CPU-bound work to the thread pool and returns a Task, e.g. to keep a UI thread responsive?
questions.explanation: `await Task.Run(() => Crunch())` moves the work off the UI thread. Don't wrap I/O in `Task.Run`: truly async I/O methods already don't block a thread. `Task.FromResult` wraps an existing value; `Task.Yield` just reschedules the continuation.

questions.prompt: Why should you avoid `async void` methods (outside event handlers)?
questions.answer: The caller can't await them or catch their exceptions; an exception is rethrown on the synchronization context and usually crashes the process.
distractors: They run synchronously and block the caller.
questions.explanation: An `async Task` method stores its exception in the Task for the awaiter. An `async void` method has nowhere to put it, so it's raised directly on the context (or the thread pool) and takes down the app. 'Silently swallowed' is closer to an un-awaited `async Task`.

questions.prompt: Which type is a lighter alternative to `Task<T>` that avoids a heap allocation when the result is usually available synchronously?
questions.explanation: `ValueTask<T>` is a struct that can hold a ready result directly, so a cached hit costs no allocation. The trade-off: await it exactly once and don't await it concurrently. Default to `Task<T>` unless profiling says otherwise.

questions.prompt: Which type do you pass into an async method so the caller can ask it to stop early?
questions.explanation: The caller owns a `CancellationTokenSource` (which can `Cancel()`), and passes its `Token` down. Methods receive only the token, so they can observe cancellation but not trigger it. Pass it on to every async call you make.
